extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th-century nonfiction chapter diagnosing urban social problems (lodging-houses, Chinatown, Jewtown) and offering prescriptive observations and remedies for public-health, policing, charity, and immigration policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot reform as remedy for lodging-house electoral corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Real ballot reform will do more to knock out cheap lodging-houses than all the regulations of police and health officers together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lodging-houses are described as favorite recruiting grounds for political bosses; corruption at polls originates in these houses. Therefore, fixing the voting system (ballot reform) is recommended as a more effective remedy than merely policing or health regulations. Examples: lodging-houses supplying voters by the 'barrel'; occasional prosecutions are largely spectacular and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design charity experiments with capacity planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Charitable relief offerings must account for potential demand spikes—an experiment giving free coffee and rolls grew from a dozen to 2,014 in two weeks and had to close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot philanthropic efforts should anticipate rapid growth in demand and include scalable staffing/space and rules to prevent collapse of the service. The anecdote warns that well-intentioned charity without capacity can be overwhelmed and fail to answer the underlying problem (estimating the number of tramps remained unsolved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Family-based immigration condition to promote social stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the door wider for his wife; make it a condition of his coming or staying that he bring his wife with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that requiring or encouraging immigrants to arrive with family (wives) would promote domestic stability and reduce social ills attributed to bachelor immigrant populations (e.g., vice, homelessness). Presented as a policy prescription to improve assimilation and reduce the 'real Chinese question.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Active public-health surveillance for hidden disease nests
rubrics_metrics.description: Health officers should be on constant and sharp lookout for hidden fever-nests (typhus, small-pox) in overcrowded tenements and workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tenement homes double as workshops and clothing manufactured there can spread disease (e.g., small-pox and typhus patients found among garments destined for sale), public-health practice must include vigorous inspection, search for concealed sick, and tracing of disease sources. Example: children recovering from small-pox found among half-finished clothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic hygiene education for children (school exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily school exercise: 'What must I do to be healthy?' — 'I must keep my skin clean, Wear clean clothes, Breathe pure air, And live in the sunlight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachable, repeatable hygiene rules are recommended as part of elementary instruction to counteract ignorance of cleanliness that contributes to disease. The exercise is given as a model pedagogical rubric for instilling hygienic habits in children coming from unsanitary tenement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate overcrowded tenement home-work conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Homes of the Hebrew quarter are also workshops; dozens of people may work in a single small room, creating filth diseases and spreading contagion through goods made there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and regulation should address the combined living-and-working conditions (ventilation, space, sanitary practices) because production of ready-made clothing in infected rooms can distribute contagion widely. Suggested focus: reduce density, separate work from living quarters, improve ventilation and sanitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe scrutiny and vigorous policing in secretive colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: The severest official scrutiny, the harshest repressive measures are justifiable in Chinatown, orderly as it appears on the surface, because its secrecy and internal code obstruct investigation and foster serious social harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because covert group behavior (shielding criminals, collective silence) and clandestine activities (gambling notices on telegraph pole, fan tan, opium dens) hinder ordinary policing, the author argues for intensified investigative pressure and enforcement in such neighborhoods. Examples: difficulty tracing murders and the collective action to shield criminals.
